claim: The flat-combining `Store::mutateShard` queue is obsolete because the per-table snapshot+log reference protocol replaced the root-shard mutation path; intra-server serialization is now the per-table `CasSingleWriterSlot` ref-append lane, and the `CasShard*` ProfileEvents were deleted during the 2026-07-12 stabilization iteration.

Before the queue, soak workloads reached 156 concurrent shard-mutating threads within one second, producing 637k `casPut` attempts for 380k landed mutations, a 40% average conflict rate and 92% conflict rate during storms.

`mutateShard` is synchronous for its caller, so every queued mutation is a blocked thread waiting on a promise and the total queued items across all shards is bounded by the number of concurrently writing threads.

The shard mutation queue is owned by `Store` as one `std::unordered_map<ShardKey, ShardMutationQueue>` protected by one `std::mutex`; an idle queue entry is created by its first waiter and erased by the leader after draining, so an idle pool has no persistent per-prefix queue structures.

The caller that inserts into an idle shard queue becomes its leader; the leader repeatedly carves a batch prefix under the map mutex, releases the mutex for one read-apply-all-CAS cycle, completes promises, and then repeats until the queue is empty.
A queue batch stops before a second mutation of the same `Ref` name and before any `WholeShard` item; `WholeShard` operations such as trim, the GC fence, and `dropNamespace` flush alone.

The queue leader increments `root.shard_version` after every closure in queue order rather than once per flush, so each promise receives its own post-bump transition version and one `casPut` may carry multiple ordered events.

Before applying each queued closure, the leader snapshots the in-memory `RootShard`; if the closure throws, the snapshot is restored, that promise receives the exception, and the remaining batch items continue.
A cross-server CAS conflict causes the queue leader to re-read and re-apply all not-yet-completed closures, while exhaustion of `MAX_CAS_ATTEMPTS` fails every promise in the batch.
`mayMutate` is checked on every flush attempt; if the fence trips, the whole batch fails with `ABORTED` and no caller receives a successful mutation.
When a batched final body exceeds the hard limit, the queue degrades to single-item re-flushes so only the offending mutation receives `LIMIT_EXCEEDED` and innocent mutations proceed.
A create-if-absent mutation with `token == nullopt` flushes alone using its `birth_incarnation` and `birth_floor_provider`, preserving the existing birth-stamping behavior.
The queue leader holds the shared side of `view_gate` for the entire flush, so a batch remains one in-flight mutation for the beat and drain protocol.
GC trim uses `mutateShard` as a `WholeShard` queue item, so trim rewrites no longer race writers even though trim still flushes alone.

The queue's TLA+ posture treats a batch as a sequence of today's transitions committed atomically; any crash or conflict leaves a durable prefix, and the reachable durable states are a subset of those available from fast sequential `casPut` operations.

AWS S3 conforms to the CAS backend requirements: capability probing observes honest 412 responses for wrong-token conditional operations, two-phase reclaim deletes objects physically, and fsck remains clean through more than 28 GC rounds.

On the AWS validation stand, reclaim progressed from 11 condemned objects in round 24 to graduation in round 26 and deletion of all 11 in round 27; after reclaim fsck reported `dangling=0 unreachable=0 unaccounted=0`.

Live AWS S3 GC rounds took 30–40 seconds, compared with about 5–10 seconds on RustFS; the shipped default `gc_interval_sec=60` is sane for AWS, while a 10-second soak interval causes back-to-back rounds.
The metadata factory silently overrode the intended 32 `root_shards` with a default of 8; changing the factory default to 32 was verified live with shard indexes up to 27.
A server configuration template can expand `<server_root_id>{replica}</server_root_id>` per replica using the same macro expansion as the S3 `endpoint`.
Probe cleanup must be HEAD-gated before issuing `deleteExact`; otherwise AWS returns 400 `InvalidArgument` when cleanup sends an empty `If-Match` after the probe keys were already deleted.
Conditional deletes performed by `removeObjectIfTokenMatches` are recorded by `BlobStorageLogWriter` for all outcomes, with the S3 error attached when applicable.

A CAS container recreated without persistent `/var/lib/clickhouse` gets a new `ServerUUID`, and the pool correctly refuses the foreign root claim with `CORRUPTED_DATA`; the refusal reports both UUIDs and three recovery paths.
`/var/lib/clickhouse` must be persistent, such as on a PVC, because its local UUID file is the CAS identity.
The removed configuration keys `content_addressed_gc_grace_sec` and `content_addressed_allow_shared_pool` are not parsed and must not appear in soak configurations.
The GCS S3-compatible endpoint silently ignores `If-None-Match`, `If-Match` overwrite, and `If-Match` delete preconditions; notably, a wrong-ETag DELETE can delete the object.
GCS XML API with GOOG4-HMAC-SHA256 signing enforces the required conditional operations, using `x-goog-if-generation-match` and returning `x-goog-generation` as the token.

GCS `CompleteMultipartUpload` silently ignores `x-goog-if-generation-match`, so conditional writes must not use multipart there; `Compose` enforces the precondition, making multipart-to-temp-key followed by `Compose(temp -> final)` and temp deletion the production path for large blobs.

Native GCS Generation binding requires GOOG4 signing, precondition mapping from `If-None-Match: *` to `x-goog-if-generation-match: 0` and from `If-Match: <etag>` to `x-goog-if-generation-match: <generation>`, plus extraction from `x-goog-generation`; this was identified as a design implication but was not started in the initial probe run.

The GCS Generation binding was implemented with a GOOG4 signer, wire-boundary conditional dialect, `http_client = gcs_hmac`, `TokenType::Generation`, single-PUT guard, and fail-closed probe versioning; a live cycle passed probe, replication, reclaim, fsck, and logged 100 deletes with zero errors.

On GCS, non-numeric probe wrong tokens caused the dialect format guard to fail closed; LIST-derived MD5 ETags poisoned `If-Match` in GC and are disabled on generation stores; and `Expect: 100-continue` initially missed the dialect header, creating a B118-class stall risk.
Azure validation was not started, and GCS production follow-ups remain desirable: Compose finalization for writes larger than 1 GiB, `gcp_oauth` validation, and generation-aware LIST discovery.
A 100 GiB final merge was streaming rather than memory-materialized: both replicas reached about 115 MiB RSS during `OPTIMIZE FINAL`.

The CAS write path spills the entire object to local `cas_scratch` for hash-before-upload, so writing a part requires free local disk at least as large as the part even though the S3 upload streams; the proposed fix is in-stream hashing.

Two replicas performing the same shared-pool `OPTIMIZE FINAL` independently can double-spill roughly one full part size each even though deduplication retains one pool blob; a shared-pool replica could adopt the already-uploaded blob instead of re-merging locally.

The 24 GiB S01 rerun passed streaming, multipart, deduplication, replica agreement, fsck, and GC checks, but recorded 41,983 `S3HeadObject` operations for one table, 13,116 read errors out of 69,187 reads, and 717 write errors out of 8,330 writes.

The scenario scratch high-water sampler was not reliable at scale because its 2-second interval missed the `OPTIMIZE FINAL` spike; direct measurement found 93 GiB while the sampler reported 0.100 GiB.

The corrected S02 workload uses deterministic incompressible `generateRandom('payload String', <seed>, per_row) LIMIT rows` data with `max_threads=1`, so duplicate inserts exercise the real large-blob `dedup_head_first_min_bytes` path.
Idle GC over a static 20M-row, 400-part pool used about 1,362 `CasGcGet`, 643 `CasBlobHead`, and 457 `CasRootGet` operations per round, roughly 2,500 S3 operations per round despite no changes.

The observed GC round duration grew from 87 ms at 400 parts to 92.6 seconds at 10,000 tables and 398 seconds at 100,000 parts, demonstrating O(ref-universe/object-count) scaling; fsck also becomes O(objects) and timed out at 100,000 parts.

For a 10,000-table pool, GC startup cost is O(table/ref count): observed root metadata reads were `CasRootList=110255` and `CasRootGet=42127`, about 152,000 S3 operations, while recovery remained 64 seconds because it did not enumerate blobs.

The flat-combining shard queue reduced S08 contention to 8 conflicts across 702,172 mutations, while 100,000 parts were created successfully and root-shard objects stayed bounded at at most 8 per namespace.

A background merge can rewrite payload inside S09's mutation measurement window and falsely report pool growth; consolidating with `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL` before establishing the baseline isolates mutation carry-forward, while `SYSTEM STOP MERGES` also stops mutations because they use the merge scheduler.

S10's authoritative delete oracle confirmed correct deletes; a bucket can be repopulated by later inserts because each insert writes all 100 buckets, so a final `ALTER DELETE ... mutations_sync=2` is required to test removal without that confound.
Partitioned inserts in S11 require O(partitions) CAS commits, taking about 10 seconds for a 256-partition insert; deferred GC during 64 delete rounds allowed orphaned parts to outpace disk capacity.

Rapid repeated crash-restart in S13 could wedge mount-lease self-adoption with `key '...ca_soak_ch1/mount' was touched while adopting our own mount slot`; the node stayed down with exit code 49 until the mount object was manually deleted.

A clean restart of both servers with 10,000 tables recovered all tables in 64.2 seconds, with no unknown-disk false positives and `CasBlobList=0` at startup; the rapid-kill S13 wedge is not a normal graceful-restart failure.

The full-scale P0 campaign found six O(N) cost families: GC round O(pool objects), scratch equal to full part size, replicated `OPTIMIZE` double-spill, wide-part O(columns), partitioned INSERT O(partitions), and startup O(refs).

Unversioned RustFS overwrites of objects larger than 128 KiB leak the previous data directory; scanner reclamation found zero files after more than two hours, and LIST operations timed out around 600,000 files.

The prior soak recorded 8.7 million `CasBlobHead` operations, 380k landed `CasOtherCas` shard writes, 257k conflict attempts, and 1.29 million `CasOtherGet` operations per replica in one hour; shard bodies were 250–340 KB and 95% of a typical 3157-event body was journal tail, while later fsck timeouts belonged to the leak-bloated LIST family tracked by B146 and B154.

`Build::copyForwardFromCondemned` incorrectly verified payloads with one-shot `CityHash128`, while the pool uses streaming `HashingWriteBuffer` hashing in 2048-byte blocks (`DBMS_DEFAULT_HASHING_BLOCK_SIZE`); payloads larger than 2048 bytes were falsely rejected.
Copy-forward verification must recompute the content hash with `HashingReadBuffer` over the payload and the same `getHexUIntLowercase` to `hexToU128` conversion used by the write path.

The shard-mutation queue implementation completed with 200,675 mutations compressed into 87,594 `casPut` operations, a 2.3x compression ratio, and only 11 intra-server reference conflicts; `CasOtherCas` equaled flushes.

The queue implementation needed identity-checked map-entry erasure because a slow waiter could otherwise erase a successor queue by key and create two leaders with conflicts; test counters also had to exclude bootstrap and mount-renewal `casPut` operations.

GC rebuild initially missed physical blobs with zero rebuilt edges because they had no run row and never transitioned to zero; the rebuild now condemns such blobs directly using head-captured tokens, a minted round, and floor-gated graduation.

The validated CAS defaults are `root_shards=32` for the server default, 64 shards in soak configurations, and `gc_trim_body_soft_limit=8 MiB`; the 96 KiB experiment could not constrain the cursor-age-bound journal tail, while the 256-event count gate remains the effective trimmer.

With `root_shards=8` and a 96 KiB trim cap, observed shard bodies still reached 588 KB because the tail above the sealed cursor is round-cadence-bound; one key accumulated 8,471 leaked RustFS directories in 30 minutes.

A GC safety bug allowed clamped shards to skip landed events: a blob was deleted while its landed `+1` remained unfolded, yielding 31 dangling blobs and one dangling manifest; this violated INV-NO-LOSS.

If any fold pass records a clamp anomaly, destruction is suppressed: no graduations or redeletes occur, pending entries carry `UNCHANGED`, condemn/spare continue, and deletes resume on the first clamp-free pass; the pass emits a warning and increments `CasGcClampSuppressedPasses`.

The clamped-shard incident was caused by RustFS false 404s on `HEAD` during a `rustfs#3231` metacache storm; the false 404s produced clamps, and clamp suppression prevented graduation over unfolded events until the storm ended.
The `gc_fold_clamp` event records namespace, shard, manifest, reason, and `at_version`, making clamp forensics queryable instead of requiring archived server-log archaeology.
GC Lever A skips the expensive in-degree snapshot rebuild on rounds with no destructive decision; Lever B, an incremental point-updatable in-degree store, remains out of scope.

`Gc::fold` performs a streaming two-cursor merge over the entire prior generation's source-edge run, reading the whole prior generation and writing a whole new consolidated run even when one edge or no edge changed.

The DEFER decision is true exactly when changed-shard count is below `fold_threshold`, no destructive decision is due, and `rounds_since_last_fold` is below `gc_fold_max_defer_rounds`; otherwise the round FOLDs.

DEFER leaves the sealed `(snap_generation, snap_attempt)` unchanged, so journals accumulate naturally from the old sealed cursor and a later FOLD processes the accumulated deltas without new persisted accumulator state.

The pre-fold DEFER decision uses only O(shards) `LIST(cas/refs/)` token-diff signals, O(retired-entries + servers) graduation-due signals, and an O(1) defer window; it does not read journals or inspect whether a changed shard contains `+1` or `−1` content.

A deferred owner removal is conservative because the stale in-degree is too high and can only delay reclaim, whereas a deferred owner addition is dangerous if a pending blob graduates from a stale zero in-degree snapshot.

The load-bearing GC safety invariant is: no destructive decision is ever made on a not-fully-folded snapshot; any pending-delete graduation forces a FOLD before deletion so a protective `+1` is observed.
A new zero-in-degree condemnation candidate discovered during DEFER is detected only at the next FOLD, delaying reclaim by at most the bounded defer window but never deleting an uncondemned blob.
`gc_fold_max_defer_rounds` bounds batching so every accumulated delta is folded within a bounded number of rounds; a due destructive decision also forces a FOLD.

DEFER does not write `gc/state` or advance the round and uses a leader-local in-memory `rounds_since_last_fold`; the lease-renew CAS still runs because it is required to retain leadership and heartbeat liveness.

The default `gc_fold_threshold = 1` preserves today's behavior for changed rounds and defers only zero-delta idle rounds; `gc_fold_max_defer_rounds = 8` is inert at threshold 1 and matters when batching is enabled with a threshold greater than 1.

The required `CaGcRoundDeferCore` TLA+ gate must establish `NoOverDelete` and `EventuallyFolded`; sabotage allowing graduation on a stale snapshot must produce a `NoOverDelete` counterexample, and sabotage removing the defer bound must produce an `EventuallyFolded` counterexample.

The GC acceptance criteria require idle rounds to perform no generation-run reads or writes, small-delta rounds to amortize snapshot rebuilds, default behavior to remain unchanged except for idle skipping, and `dangling == 0` in unit and live validation.

`PoolConfig::gc_fold_threshold` is a `uint64_t` defaulting to 1, and `PoolConfig::gc_fold_max_defer_rounds` is a `uint64_t` defaulting to 8; the pure predicate is `shouldDeferRound(size_t, bool, uint64_t, uint64_t, uint64_t)`.

`graduationDue` returns true for a retired entry with `delete_pending` or `condemn_round < min_ack`; a missing retired list also returns true to force the existing fail-closed fold path rather than silently deferring.
`changedShardCount` is the number of present shards whose token differs from the sealed generation, represented by the non-`DiscoverDecision::Skip` decisions from `computeDiscoverDecisions`.

A deferred GC round reports `RoundReport::deferred=true`, emits a round event with `outcome = "deferred"`, and leaves the sealed generation pinned without fold, delete, or round-commit CAS; a FOLD resets the leader-local defer counter.

The CAS harness's transport probes are best-effort: failures return `None` or an empty sentinel rather than raising, and a scenario that requires a missing observation must be marked inconclusive rather than pass silently.

After the per-server-tree relocation, manifests live under `cas/manifests/<srid>/...` and refs under `cas/refs/<srid>/...`; the old classifiers placed the tree in `other`, causing S08 to report 858081 objects and 138 GB as `other` and allowing a real manifest leak to pass the leftover verdict.

`classify_pool_path` recognizes pool-relative and prefixed keys and returns one of `blobs`, `_manifests`, `refs`, `roots`, `gc`, `_files`, `_pool_meta`, or `other`; `RECLAIMABLE_UNREACHABLE_PREFIXES` remains `(`"blobs"`, `"_manifests"`)`.

The harness `gc_log_rows` query used removed `forgotten_on_delete` and `forgotten_absent` columns, causing `UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER` on every poll and making every GC verdict in the 2026-07-05 campaign vacuous.

The corrected GC-log observation includes `entries_condemned`, `entries_graduated`, `entries_redeleted`, `fence_outs`, `min_ack`, and `anomalies` along with deletion, outcome, duration, and error fields.

`settle_fsck` stabilizes on `(reachable, dangling)` and intentionally excludes `unreachable`, because background GC legitimately churns unreachable objects; convergence of unreachable is owned by `forced_gc_to_fixpoint`.

`s3_error_rates(node)` reports read/write error and request counters plus rates, returning `None` when counters are absent rather than fabricating zero; `end_checkpoint` stores the rates as an informational verdict.
The harness field `cont_mem_peak_incl_cache` is explicitly cache-inclusive cgroup memory evidence; verdicts use `peak_mem_resident` for resident-memory claims.

CAS introspection is read-only and fail-open per row: a corrupt or racing mount body becomes a `state='corrupt'` row or is skipped, never an exception into the query; unlike `computeHeartbeatFloor`, `listMounts` performs no fence writes.
`Cas::listMounts` enumerates mount slots with one LIST and one GET per slot and classifies each as `live`, `expired`, `terminated`, `fenced`, or `corrupt`.

The planned `system.content_addressed_mounts` table has columns `disk`, `srid`, `server_uuid`, `hostname`, `pid`, `writer_epoch`, `seq`, `started_at_ms`, `expires_at_ms`, `min_active`, `observed_gc_round`, `gc_fenced`, and `state`.

Mount-slot audit adds `CasEventType::MountClaim`, `MountRelease`, and `MountConflict`, serialized as `mount_claim`, `mount_release`, and `mount_conflict`; conflict details include the observed holder UUID, hostname, PID, epoch, sequence, and expiry when available.

The first CAS `CurrentMetrics` gauges are `CasGcIsLeader` and `CasGcPendingReclaimEntries`; the former reflects whether the latest round acquired the lease, while the latter is process-local cumulative condemned entries minus executed exact-token deletes.

`FsckReport` partial mode returns accumulated lower-bound counts with `partial=true` and `partial_reason` when a deadline raises `TIMEOUT_EXCEEDED`; without partial mode the timeout exception is preserved.

`runFsck` namespace scoping uses `namespace_prefix`, checks only matching references, performs dangling-only HEAD verification of named blobs, and intentionally skips pool-wide unreachable/pending/unaccounted classification.
Before scoped and partial fsck, the scenario campaign lost five verdicts because fsck timed out at large object counts and returned no accumulated result.

The lease/view decoupling moves S3-heavy retired-view refresh off `MountLeaseKeeper::renewOnce`; renewal reads only cheap in-memory values including `Store::observedGcRound()`, while a Store-owned poller runs `Store::syncRetiredView()` independently.

The old renewal path could let a slow retired-view refresh or `view_gate` drain delay the lease PUT beyond the 30-second TTL during RustFS retry storms, causing GC to fence a fully alive server; the observed RustFS read-error rate was about 19%.

`Store::observedGcRound()` returns the currently installed `retire_view.round()` through the retired view's internal synchronization, so renewal performs local reads and one lease PUT without a `gc/state` GET.

The retired-view syncer runs `syncRetiredView()` every `mount_renew_period`, performs the `gc/state` probe and `RetireView::refresh()` only when the published round is newer, and emits `RetiredViewAdvance` only for an actual advance.

A lower `observed_gc_round` caused by syncer lag is conservative because `computeHeartbeatFloor` takes the minimum acknowledgement across live heartbeats; lag can hold the floor back but cannot advance it beyond an installed round.

Both the lease-renewal thread and retired-view syncer are gated by `background_watermark`; `Store::open` and `tryRemountOnce` synchronously call `syncRetiredView()` before starting the keeper so the first anchored lease carries a current acknowledgement.

The view-side names are `Store::syncRetiredView()` and `CasEventType::RetiredViewAdvance` with event string `retired_view_advance`; the lease-side names `MountLeaseKeeper`, `renewOnce`, `mount_renew_period`, and `SingleWriterSlot` remain unchanged.

The retired-view syncer catches and logs its own exceptions, retries on the next tick, and must be stopped and joined before `retire_view` or `pool_backend` are destroyed; renewal fail-closed behavior otherwise remains unchanged.
The mount-lease recovery protocol follows the TLA+ rule that a GC fence costs an epoch: a fenced same-epoch body is never adoptable or refreshable, and recovery always allocates a new writer epoch.
Terminating a never-started `SingleWriterSlot` is a quiet no-op, while double termination of a genuinely started slot remains an exception.
`MountClaimResult::FencedSelf` represents a same-UUID, same-epoch mount body with `gc_fenced=true`; `claimMount` must not write a refresh in that case, and a different epoch may reclaim immediately.

Renewal mismatches are classified by the current mount body: an own fenced body is reported as `fenced_by_gc`, a newer own epoch as superseded, a foreign UUID as a foreign writer, and an unexplained mismatch remains a loud fail-closed exception.

`Store::open` retries fence recovery at most three times; on `FencedSelf` or `MountFencedException` it allocates a fresh writer epoch, rebuilds the keeper, and retries, while the final `armMountFence` uses the final epoch.

After a successful mount claim, `doStart` retains one synchronous view refresh before the first lease body; the renewal background path itself is a single lease PUT and the view refresh runs on its own cadence.

The lease/view implementation splits the merged heartbeat into a cheap renewal path using `Store::observedGcRound()` and a Store-owned `syncRetiredView` poller that performs the S3-heavy work independently.
`Store::renewWatermarkOnce()` remains the composed test/manual driver that runs `syncRetiredView()` and then `mount_keeper->renewOnce()`, while production renewal uses the isolated cheap path.
`Store::observedGcRound() const` returns `retire_view.round()` as a cheap, race-safe in-memory read, and `renewLeaseOnlyForTest()` renews without synchronizing the retired view.

The Store-owned retired-view syncer exposes `startRetiredViewSync`, idempotent `stopRetiredViewSync`, and `retiredViewSyncLoop`; it waits on a condition variable, catches and logs body exceptions, and is joined during Store teardown.

The retired-view syncer starts only under `background_watermark` after the mount fence is armed and does not restart per remount because it is tied to the Store lifetime rather than a mount incarnation.
The queued flush applies the soft-limit delay once per flush whenever any batched item has `origin == Writer`, preserving the pacing intent tracked by B164b.
The shard-mutation-queue documentation plan was intended to close the B157 contention axis by recording the queue design, conflict/rewrite budget, and completed roadmap status.
The harness-honesty plan explicitly leaves B197, the product-side GC stop issue, out of scope because the plan changes only Python harness code.
The introspection package is tracked under the `B15/B99/B169` release-readiness roadmap bullet for the mounts table, mount audit events, first gauges, and scoped/partial fsck.
